exit_trigger: Evidence that OEM specification or qualification barriers are weakening and customers are switching suppliers on price; Sustained loss of pricing power, shown by falling margins while volumes hold; Faster-than-expected decline in internal-combustion engine fluid demand without offsetting growth; Management making large value-destroying acquisitions or revealing accounting problems; Debt-to-equity rising materially above 0.5 without a clear return justification; Price above 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value, persistently
rationale: I own this one, and I'm not going to sell a business with a 30.6% five-year average ROE just because the quote is 20.82% below my entry at $886.815. A lower price on an intact moat is a better price, not a worse business. The snapshot puts intrinsic value at about $1,271.73 against $702.22, a 44.78% margin of safety, but that model uses 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat it with a healthy haircut. Debt-to-equity of 0.4968 clears my 0.5 line by a hair, and that leaves no room for error. I'll keep what I own, but I won't add until I can verify the ten-year earnings record and how the product holds up as vehicles change.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand erosion: sustained loss of full-price selling power or persistent heavy discounting; Management failure: value-destroying acquisitions, dishonest or opaque reporting; Growth requiring ever-larger promotions or capital to keep the brand relevant, signalling the moat is being rebuilt each season; Price above 1.5x a conservatively re-derived intrinsic value, persistently; A materially better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: I own this one, 10 shares bought at $128.38, now $105.84, down 17.56% in 98 days. A price decline alone never made me sell a business with an intact moat, and the snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 34.6% and a reported debt-to-equity of 0.0. The model's intrinsic value of $346.97 rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat that 69.5% margin of safety as a generous upper bound, not a promise. My real worry is the one I have about any apparel brand: is this a lasting brand with pricing power, or a fashion that must be rebuilt every season? The snapshot has no margin trend, no pricing data and no ten-year earnings record, so I can't settle that, and I hold without adding until I can. Time is the friend of the wonderful company, but I need evidence it is one.

exit_trigger: Franchise laws or manufacturer direct-sales models materially weaken the dealer's protected position; Sustained decline in ROE well below 15% or debt-to-equity rising above 0.5; Evidence of poor capital allocation, such as large acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices, or dishonesty by management; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; A clearly better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: I own six shares of this automotive and truck dealer, bought at $216.765 and now marked at $212.36, a loss of about 2%, and I am not going to lose sleep over that. Selling cars and trucks and servicing them is a business I understand, but I will not call the moat wonderful; it rests mostly on franchise protection and scale, not on a brand people pay up for. The snapshot gives a five-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.39 and a value of $259.62 a share on zero assumed growth, an 18.2% margin of safety, which clears my 15% bar without much room to spare. Owner earnings of about $1.09 billion against a $13.96 billion market cap is a yield near 7.8%, and I cannot confirm that clears Treasury plus 4% because the Treasury yield is not in the data. I also have no ten-year earnings record, no CEO tenure and no insider data, so I keep what I own, add nothing, and let the evidence come in.

exit_trigger: Evidence of moat erosion: sustained loss of pricing power or customer retention to large rivals or online platforms; Management failure: value-destroying acquisitions or evidence of dishonest reporting; A materially better opportunity with much higher conviction; Price above 1.5 × intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Leverage rising well beyond the current 0.35 debt-to-equity without a clear reason
rationale: We own 11 shares, bought 18 days ago at $120.05 and now down 1.32%, which tells me nothing about the business. This is an industrial supply distributor. I understand the model: stock a deep catalog, deliver fast, and earn the customer's repeat orders. The numbers I can see are good: a 5-year average ROE of 20.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, a $6.6 billion market cap, and a 24.6% margin of safety against the model's value of $157. But I'm not backing the truck up. The value rests on 8% growth against a 5% discount rate, while owner earnings are only about 4.6% of the market cap. Distribution moats are real but narrower than Coca-Cola's, so I keep the position, add nothing, and stay alert to any erosion in customer stickiness.

exit_trigger: Evidence that installers and distributors are switching to rival brands, or that the company can no longer pass through cost increases; A technology shift (heat pump or tankless) that the company fails to capture, eroding its share and returns; Sustained fall in ROE well below 15% without a clear cause; Management capital allocation failure, such as a large overpriced acquisition, or evidence of dishonesty; Price above 1.5x a re-examined intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: I own this one, and I'm content to keep owning it. A. O. Smith sells water heaters and boilers, a product nobody shops for with enthusiasm but everyone must replace, and it sells mostly through plumbers who default to a name they trust. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 23.7% with debt-to-equity of 0.083, and that is the profile of a business that doesn't need much borrowed money to earn good returns. At $64.26 against my conservative estimate of $95.72, the margin of safety is 32.9%, though I'd note the estimate leans on a 5% discount rate, so I haircut my own enthusiasm. The position is only 21 days old and up 4.5%, which proves nothing; I'm holding on the economics, not the quarter, and the gaps in my checking (10-year earnings record, management tenure) keep me from adding aggressively.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained price cuts or share loss to private-label products; Management pursuing large, expensive acquisitions or loading the balance sheet with debt; Verification showing true leverage well above the reported debt-to-equity of 0.0027 and above 0.5; Price sustained above 1.5x intrinsic value with no growth in owner earnings; Discovery of accounting irregularities or dishonest communication
rationale: We own this one, and I see no reason to fiddle with it after fifteen days. Paint, sealants and protective coatings are a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and the brands sit on the shelf and in the contractor's habits. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 22.9% and an estimated intrinsic value of about $133.59 against a price near $102.70, a 23.1% margin of safety, which clears my 15% bar. I do hold some reservations: the 5% discount rate and 8% growth cap make the valuation sensitive, and the reported debt-to-equity of 0.0027 looks too low for me to accept without checking the filing. I'll keep the shares, not add on this evidence alone, and let time do the work. Being down 0.84% after two weeks tells me nothing about the business.

exit_trigger: Evidence that the cost and scale advantage is eroding, such as sustained loss of share to lower-cost imports or substitutes; Return on equity falling persistently toward market-average levels; Management makes value-destroying acquisitions or shows a lack of candor; Price rising well above 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Discovery that debt is materially higher than the reported 0.0 debt-to-equity suggests
rationale: We own 24 shares, bought eight days ago at $54.285, so the question is whether to keep them, not whether to open the position. The numbers in front of me are handsome: a 5-year average ROE of 29.3%, a reported debt-to-equity of 0.0, and a $6.04B market cap that clears my size bar. The model says $168.53 a share, but that rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on a figure that generous. A copper-products maker is a business close to a commodity, and its moat is scale and cost position rather than a brand that lets it raise prices at will. I'm holding, not adding, until I can verify the 10-year earnings record and the management record, which this snapshot does not provide.

exit_trigger: Loss of or material delay in a flagship Navy shipbuilding program; Persistent contract cost overruns that show the franchise lacks pricing power; Sustained cut in naval shipbuilding budgets that cannot be offset; Management capital allocation that destroys value, such as acquisitions or buybacks at peak prices
rationale: I don't own this one, and the snapshot doesn't give me enough to start. A builder of Navy warships has a real franchise: almost nobody else can build these vessels, and the customer is the U.S. government. But that is one customer, set by budgets and contract terms I can't see here. The screen shows a 46% margin of safety, but it rests on 8% growth for a decade, which is more than I would lean on for a business whose revenue comes from appropriations. It also shows debt-to-equity of 0.0, and I won't believe a shipbuilder has no debt until I see the balance sheet, because an untagged number is not a debt-free company. I'll wait until I can verify ten years of earnings and the debt, and then decide. No hurry.
